teacher_info.introduction:
When I was 12, I started a 3-year school programme where 80% of my classes were in French.The first day, I felt so stupid because I couldn't understand anything--but everyone else had an answer for the teacher. On the bus home, my friend told me that they were only saying "I don't know" or "I don't understand" in French. 

This taught me 2 valuable lessons: first, it wasn't true that everyone was a better French speaker than me, and second, I needed to find some techniques for situations where I couldn't explain what I wanted to say. Now that I'm on the other side, teaching people to speak English, I still think back to those two lessons. 

Confidence is key to improving our fluency, so I won't attack every mistake--only if they make it hard to understand you. I also try to give students ideas for phrases or strategies for when they don't know the words in English. 

I love to meet new people and learn about their part of the world. So I started studying Spanish in 2012. In 2014, my partner and I quit our jobs to spend 4 months studying Spanish in Peru, and 5 more months travelling around South America to practise. Wow! We met so many interesting people, and learned so much more about each place than we could have without Spanish. Another lesson I learned here was, practise makes perfect. In our classes, we studied all sorts of vocabulary, grammar, and the verbs! So many verb tenses! When we left Peru, I could say very complicated sentences. But as we travelled, we used simple grammar; where we were from, where we were going, how much was the taxi, when was the bus... And by the time we got back to the UK, I'd forgotten all those complicated verbs! 

Students need opportunities to practise different vocabulary, different grammar, different types of English. I ask my students to look at videos or articles from all over; the news, entertainment, culture, sports. All of these give us different ways to use English, and learn new things about our world.

I come from Australia, but I speak with Received Pronunciation, a "correct/standard" form of British English, but very much a NEUTRAL accent, which I think is important to be understood in whatever country you are living in.

Writing a song in English is not just a question of translating it from your own language. We want it to sound good - we need to think of good/cool expressions; find words that rhyme or sound similar, and keep in mind the number of syllables so that it conforms to the beat.
Sometimes we need to look for alternative words to avoid difficult sustained notes at the end of a line, such as the long "ee" sound. An example of this is the song, "And I am telling you", in particular the Jennifer Hudson version.
For singers, I can also help you with pronunciation. So, if you're interested in breaking into the English market, or just as a hobby, let's get writing!

pro_course_detail.title: Starting Ancient Greek
pro_course_detail.description:
I take a very traditional approach to teaching this language. It is grammar forward, but if you are afraid of grammar (as so many people seem to be these days), have no fear. You can do it.  I did it.

When I first did Ancient Greek, I knew no grammar, even though I had brilliant ideas and spoke very well. My essays were full of basic grammatical errors. Ancient Greek was the tool that opened my eyes to grammar and inspired me to love learning languages. I want to share this inspiration with you too.

Although I really want to share my passion for the Classical Attic Greek of Euripides, Aristophanes, and Plato, if you have your heart set on biblical Greek (Koine), I can help with that too. Koine was my first teaching job, actually. But there are sections in the bible that slide into classical grammar, and if you only learn koine, you will struggle.  If you learn learn Attic Greek first, koine is easy to read.
